newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK's own doubts weigh heavy in EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK's own doubts weigh heavy in EMU debate.

text.p: Britain is expected to fare no worse than many other EU states on meeting the criteria for a single currency, but the big question is still whether it will bite the political bullet and join.

Two polls by Reuters of forecasts for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) published on Monday showed that while Britain may come up to scratch on its economy, it is likely to count itself out of membership at the start by its own hesitation.
"As long as Britain is hedging, it's going to be out," said international economist Steven Englander of Smith Barney in Paris. "No one's going to make an exception for the U.K."

Britain's ruling Conservatives, facing a general election by May next year and trailing in opinion polls, are bitterly divided over the country's role in Europe and whether to forfeit the pound sterling for the euro. They are committed to consulting Britons in a referendum before joining.

Prime Minister John Major said at a Franco-British summit in Bordeaux earlier this month that the country was moving towards the criteria set by the Maastricht treaty for EMU and this would allow it to decide nearer the time whether to join the union.
The opposition Labour party, favourite to take power after the vote, said at the weekend that if it won it, too, would hold a referendum before taking Britain in.
Gordon Brown, the party's economics spokesman, said it was clear crucial aspects of EMU would not be settled in time for Labour to make up its mind before the election.

A Reuters poll of forecasts from 34 banks and institutions around Europe conducted last week showed Britain missing two out of five criteria -- not re-joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism currency grid by the end of this year, and not taming its budget deficit enough to fall below three percent of GDP.
A majority of respondents thought the country would meet the discipline of Maastricht's demands on the other criteria governing inflation, long-term interest rates and the proportion of debt to GDP.

But Britain was not alone in the poll in being expected to fail two measures out of five. Even Germany, along with front-runners for founder membership Austria, Belgium and the Netherlands, failed two out of five.
Greece failed all five criteria while Luxembourg alone would sail through all of the EMU demands, the poll predicted.
Europe will choose the founder members of monetary union early in 1998 based on how each performs on key economic measures in 1997.
"If EMU goes forward, and we think it will, there'll be no way Britain can resist being in. Such a big economy can't stand alone," said Nomura International bond strategist Sonja Gibbs in London.

But hardly anyone questioned in a separate Reuters survey carried out at the same time thought Britain would be there at the start. Britain was chosen by just three out of 41 economists and political analysts who took part in this poll to name the first wave countries for EMU in 1999.
But the door had not yet closed for Britain to go in at some point.
For Britain, as for many others facing the EMU test, the decision will ultimately be one of politics.

"Britain is regarded as an irritant in the sense that we keep finding fault and putting hurdles in the path of EMU but if they could do something about it, I'm quite sure...pro-Europe politicians would try and get Britain involved as far as possible," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at BankAmerica in London.
